searchText: In theory, the 21,000 accounts for looking up the source account, reading account balance, writing account balance, looking up destination account, reading account balance, updating account balance. Oh, and also reading and updating nonce. It *should* appropriately account for all of that plus the miscellaneous stuff like signature validation. Oh, and code lookup as well. See this great post: https://ethresear.ch/t/should-storage-be-priced-separately-from-execution/9101 Is there a way to use smart contract recovery wallet without increasing the cost of every tx through that wallet? imo major reason people dont use them The cost of routing through the wallet isn't that high. One storage read, no storage writes, and a delegate call. That should be on the order of single digit thousands of gas total in overhead. This is compared to a single storage write (of which, an ERC20 transfer will do at least 2) which is 5,000 to 20,000 each. Woah Wallet I've tried are more expensive Is there a place where I can find total gas usage per day, per contract for each opcode? Recent example: 8097 gas overhead. So that's 8% overhead over uniswap trade, 16% overhead over ERC20 transfer. Not sure how many users like or don't like that. 10,485 overhead for a uniswap swap via the UI, 131,712 for the rest. So 108% seems about right in that case. Ah, looks like two storage reads and a CALL for most transactions. Plus copying around the calldata, which can add up in some cases. Also, it would require you to periodically move all your assets or change your owner. We discussed only witness encryption I guess, not the simpler methods. Why is it not used? Witness encryption based on a blockchain timestamp is the only type I know of that actually gives a guarantee of time. Wait my bad, multisig still increases cost. excerpts.author: michaelrycroft
excerpts.content:
<@!301186049323958275> Many thanks for the link to the Recoverable Wallet repo, it’s certainly a possible solution for additional security against loss, But I was hoping for a more integrated solution across the whole eco system.
The thought I was having (good or bad) is more like a ledger within a ledger, the inner ledger being part of Ether itself and the outer dealing with the total balances/transactions.
Kind of like how cash money is, although bank notes are identical to one another, they all have uniqueness thanks to a serial number which can be traced back to find the notes creator/creation date.
The thought was instead of serial numbers you could store identifiers to the current owner and all previous owners, then the ability to receive or transfer (re-identify) would be limited to the identified(owner) of the currency. For example, in a transaction the recipient’s wallet only accepts currency with the recipient’s own unique identifier marked as the owner, so a re-identification process is required by the sender before any transfer can occur, in all probability with additional authorization steps to re-identify. Wouldn’t this at least stop somebody from being able to steal everything inside a wallet if they gained unauthorized access through a private key.
The only possible way to bypass this is if the private key was compromised and they also have the credentials to re-identify the currency before transferring it to themselves. Right now, some wallets have extra security methods before a transfer can be made, but is a moot point if the private key is compromised.
